content.text: loading="lazy"

tells the browser to wait until an image is close to the viewport, and it can't know that before the CSS has arrived and layout has run. For the hero image, usually the page's LCP element, that wait is pure delay. Lazy-load what's below the fold, and let the hero load eagerly, straight from the HTML, with
fetchpriority="high"
as a hint.
A performance sprint adds
loading="lazy"
to every

through a shared image component. Image bytes drop, and the landing page's LCP gets worse. We rebuilt the page and loaded it in headless Chromium 156 on a 412px-wide viewport, with the network emulated at 150 ms latency and 1.6 Mbps through the DevTools protocol, and a stylesheet from a server that takes 600 ms to answer. Over five runs, the median LCP was 1.77 s with an eager hero and 2.42 s with a lazy one. The eager hero was requested at 0.19 s; the lazy one only at 1.13 s, right after the stylesheet finished.
The common misconception
The belief: lazy-loading every image, including the one at the top of the page, always makes the page faster.

It's a reasonable generalization of good advice. Lazy loading is one attribute, it saves real bytes, and web.dev itself recommends it for offscreen images. WordPress applied it by default, shared image components often do the same, and the savings show up right away in the network panel. If deferring images is good, deferring all of them sounds even better. The catch is that "lazy" isn't free for an image that's visible the moment the page appears.
What actually happens
Lazy means "wait for a condition"
The HTML Standard defines the lazy state of the
loading

attribute as deferring the fetch until some conditions are met, and eager, the default, as fetching immediately. In practice the condition is distance from the viewport: Chrome starts a lazy image once it's within 1,250px on fast connections or 2,500px on slower ones, so images arrive just before the user scrolls to them.
The browser can't measure distance before layout

To know how far an image is from the viewport, the browser needs its position, and that takes layout, which waits for render-blocking CSS. web.dev's LCP guide says it directly: with lazy loading, the resource won't load until after layout confirms the image is in the viewport.
An eager image doesn't wait. The browser's
preload scanner

finds it in the HTML while the document is still arriving and requests it alongside the stylesheet. That's what our run showed: the eager hero downloaded during the 600 ms the stylesheet took, and the lazy hero started only once the stylesheet had arrived and layout had placed it. Chromium also requested the lazy hero at Low priority and raised it to High afterward.
Where the delay lands in LCP
web.dev splits
LCP

into four parts: time to first byte, resource load delay, resource load duration and element render delay. Lazy loading inflates the second. The guide's rule of thumb is that the LCP resource should start loading at the same time as the first resource the page loads, and its warning is blunt: never lazy-load your LCP image, because it always adds unnecessary resource load delay.

The field data agrees. web.dev joined HTTP Archive pages with CrUX data: the median page without lazy loading had a 75th percentile LCP of 2,922 ms, against 3,546 ms for the median page with it. The authors stress that's a correlation, not proof of cause, but their lab test on WordPress found the same trade: fewer image bytes, later LCP.
Lazy loading still earns its place below the fold

The fix isn't to drop the attribute everywhere. In the same WordPress study, lazy-loading only below-the-fold images completely reversed the LCP regression, partly because those images no longer compete with the hero for the network. We saw that too: with
loading="lazy"
removed from four product images far down the page, they downloaded alongside the hero and LCP rose to 3.97 s, on a local HTTP/1.1 server.
fetchpriority is a hint for when images compete
The HTML Standard describes
fetchpriority="high"

as signaling a high-priority fetch relative to other resources of the same type. web.dev calls it a hint, not a directive, and reports LCP in a Google Flights test improving from 2.6 s to 1.9 s. On our page, with only one image competing, it made no measurable difference: it pays off when several images compete. Keep it to one or two images; web.dev notes that hinting more makes it unhelpful.

✅ Right

content.text: To catch a lazy LCP image on real pages, web.dev suggests a
PerformanceObserver
check. This one logged a warning in our run for the lazy version only:

rows.text: The hero, likely the LCP element
Found by the preload scanner, requested with the first resources
Other images in the first viewport
Visible on arrival: web.dev says always eager-load them
Saves bytes and keeps the network free for the hero
A hero set as a CSS background
Not discoverable from the HTML unless preloaded

content.text: Lighthouse 13.6.0's "LCP request discovery" insight checks this directly. On our lazy version it failed three checks: "LCP resources shouldn't use loading=lazy", "Request is discoverable in initial document" and "fetchpriority=high should be applied". The eager version passed the first two.
Libraries that keep the URL in
data-src
and copy it into
src

from script hide the image from the preload scanner entirely; web.dev lists this, images added by JavaScript, and CSS background images as the cases where the LCP resource can't be discovered from the HTML. Native
loading="lazy"
below the fold makes most of these libraries unnecessary.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find the LCP element per template

content.text: Run the observer above, or check the LCP element in the DevTools Performance panel, on mobile and desktop widths. The fold moves with the viewport, so the LCP image can differ between them.

items.title: Make the hero eager and discoverable

content.text: Remove
loading="lazy"
from it, keep its URL in a plain
src
or
srcset
in the server's HTML, and add
fetchpriority="high"

items.title: Make lazy the default below the fold only

content.text: Give your image component an explicit prop such as
priority
for above-the-fold images, instead of one global default for every image.

items.title: Measure the result in the field

content.text: Compare the 75th percentile LCP before and after the change in your real-user data, not only in one lab run.
Key takeaways

Eager images are found by the preload scanner and requested while the HTML is still arriving.
Never lazy-load the LCP image: web.dev calls it unnecessary resource load delay.
Lazy-load images below the fold, where it saves bytes and reduces competition with the hero.
